Brill chapter page could not be reached by automated download human-verification; Lund research portal carries the abstract only ('a typological profile of Northern Aslian.. spoken in southern Thailand and northern Peninsular Malaysia'); MPI PuRe item_2039462 could not be reached by automated download; The two saved files were re-read and their quotes are verbatim:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final (major) syllable of the word in all Northern Aslian languages including Ceq Wong, so affixation to the left never moves it; the same generalization is stated first-hand for the sister languages Jahai (Burenhult 2005: 38) and Maniq (Wnuk & Burenhult 2014: 972), where stress is non-contrastive, invariably final, with no secondary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in the snippet for Ceq Wong; sister-language descriptions saved here (Jahai, Maniq) explicitly report no secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the snippet; Kruspe 2009 (pp. 669, 675, snippet only) discusses Malay loans re-shaped to Ceq Wong final-syllable structure (bsiʔ 'iron' < besi, kitəʔ 'car' < kereta).
new_statements.domain_note: The Handbook statement is made for Northern Aslian as a group (Ceq Wong, Jahai, Batek, Menriq, Maniq, Kensiw, etc.), not Ceq Wong alone; word-level, isolation/citation forms implied. Snippet-level access only — no saved file, so not catalog-grade.
new_statements.identity_note: Ceq Wong = Chewong = Che' Wong = Siwang (glottocode chew1245, ISO cwg), the southern outlier of Northern Aslian in western Pahang. The Handbook statement is for Northern Aslian collectively; the two first-hand statements actually saved held by the project describe sister languages Jahai (jeha1242) and Maniq (Kensiu-related Thai variety), not Ceq Wong.

new_statements.quote: The final syllable in most Aslian languages always has the structure /CVC/. The reason for this … is that Aslian languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, seldom have suffixes, and the end of the word is therefore usually part of the root and not affected by synchronic or diachronic morphophonemic processes. Also, the final syllable is the most informative part of a word in that it always receives stress and contains the greatest phonemic variation. [p. 187, quoting Dunn et al. 2011: 300] … This is especially true of the major (i.e., stressed, word-final) vowel systems, which are mostly of a 3 x 3 type. [p. 179] … typically iambic sesquisyllabic (one-and-a-half-syllable) accentual patterns [p. 178]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Kruspe, Burenhult & Wnuk 2015 statement (word stress always fixed on the final syllable), but stated for Aslian as a whole via Dunn et al. 2011, not for Ceq Wong specifically; the work has no dedicated stress section and no Ceq Wong phonology sketch.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement: in Aslian languages generally the word-final ('major') syllable always carries the stress; words are iambic sesquisyllables with unstressed minor presyllable(s) and a stressed final CVC. No Ceq Wong-specific statement; Ceq Wong is not exempted from the generalisation.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. §4.2.2 pp. 185–186 notes claims of lexical tone in some Northern Aslian varieties (Kensiw, per Phaiboon 1984, Bishop 1996a, Hajek 2003), which Benjamin treats sceptically ('the majority of Aslian languages.. lack lexical tone'); Ceq Wong is not among the varieties for which tone has been claimed.
new_statements.identity_note: Benjamin 2012 is a survey of the whole Aslian family (Northern, Central, Southern Aslian and Jah Hut); it names Ceq Wong (= Chewong, Che' Wong, Siwang) as a Northern Aslian language socially outside the Semang mesh (pp. 148–150) but gives it no phonological sketch of its own. The stress statement is Aslian-general ('most Aslian languages'), so it covers Ceq Wong only by inclusion.
